there is insufficient data to recommend for or against any specific management of nonpregant women presenting to the emergency department with vaginal bleeding.

the management of abnormal uterine bleeding in the non-pregnant patient should include a thorough history and physical exam to determine if the patient is hemodynamically stable. If the patient is hemodynamic stable, then

the emergency physician should not attempt to diagnose the cause of abnormal bleeding in the non pregnant female, and should instead treat the bleeding with the goal of obtaining a gynecologic consultation within 24-48 hours.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most common cause of acute vaginal bleeding in a nonpregnant patient is dysfunctional uterine bleeding.
the emergency physician can be an important part of the multidisciplinary team caring for women with abnormal uterine bleeding.
the management of abnormal uterine bleeding requires an understanding of the underlying etiology of the bleeding.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a thorough history and physical exam are essential in determining the cause of vaginal bleeding.
a thorough history, focused physical examination, and a limited number of laboratory tests can help guide the diagnosis and appropriate disposition of the patient with abnormal vaginal bleeding.
emergency clinicians should not be hesitant to treat patients with abnormal uterine bleeding with oral or intramuscular progesterone or estrogen.
